title: A Covington power plant for one data center: the case before Georgia's Public Service Commission
linkText: A Covington power plant for one data center

status.text: Open case at the Georgia Public Service Commission

disclosure: Drafted with AI help from the sources below. Every sentence links to its source or is labeled as our analysis. Checked by automated tests and independent AI reviewers. This is a test page; no person reviewed it.

units.t: Nearby residents and a nonprofit filed a case at the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC), which regulates utilities.
The filers ask whether VoltaGrid's plant for one data center breaks either of two laws, and seek an order to stop any violation.
VoltaGrid says the PSC has no power here and seeks dismissal.
Petitioners say the plant pollutes Newton County; Georgia EMC says its members may be affected.
The PSC's Hearing Officer holds a hearing Dec 9, 2026.
No final vote is set.
units.note: process note; the amended schedule ends with the Dec 9 hearing (P-018), and no order we read sets a vote

The petition says the state Environmental Protection Division (EPD), which issues air permits, sent VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, a notice of violation for building before it had a permit.
The notice told VoltaGrid to stop building pollution sources until a permit is issued.
Sustainable Newton, a Newton County nonprofit, and nearby residents filed the petition.

The PSC's staff, the petitioners, Georgia EMC and Georgia Power each answered VoltaGrid's request to dismiss.

units.t: The petitioners answered the appeal, and a PSC staff witness filed rebuttal testimony.
The petition asks the Public Service Commission (PSC) to say whether the plan by VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, breaks two power laws.
The petition also asks the PSC to order VoltaGrid to stop any work that breaks those laws.
The first law is the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
The second law is the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners.
The petition says the Cogeneration Act bars the sale of a plant's power to anyone but an electric supplier.
The hearing will take up four questions.
The first is whether the PSC has power over VoltaGrid as an "electric supplier."
The second is whether the people who filed are "interested parties" who may bring the case.
The third is whether the plan to build the plant, run it and send its energy to the data center breaks either law.
The fourth is whether any PSC action is needed.
The PSC also gave the Hearing Officer, the person the PSC appointed to hear the case, a question of its own.
That question is whether VoltaGrid's service falls under the PSC's power.
If the answer is yes, the Hearing Officer is to ask "what if any action the Commission should take."
After the hearing, the Hearing Officer sends the PSC a recommended decision.
The PSC can adopt that decision.
An exhibit attached to the petition describes the plant.
The plant would make up to 90 MW from 33 natural gas engines and run all year.
One megawatt (MW) is a unit of power equal to a million watts.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: The filings we read point to three ways this Public Service Commission (PSC) case could end.
units.note: built from the petition's request (P-035), VoltaGrid's request (P-041, P-042) and the PSC's own question (P-022)

units.t: Two laws are at issue.
One is the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
The other is the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners.
This page does not pick an outcome.
units.note: nonpartisan rule

blocks.label: If you care most about neighbors' air, noise and light

units.t: The petition says VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, adds "air, light, and noise pollution to an area already overburdened by these industrial impacts."

blocks.label: If you care most about private deals between businesses

units.t: VoltaGrid says it "is the antithesis of a monopoly, and is negotiating bespoke rates with a sophisticated counterparty."

blocks.label: If you care most about who pays for stranded power lines

units.t: Georgia EMC, a trade group for electric membership corporations (EMCs), says a supplier's "other consumers" could absorb the costs if customers are "picked off."

blocks.label: If you care most about one set of rules for every power provider

units.t: Georgia Power says a one-customer exception would let any company "render any amount of service, and avoid Commission jurisdiction."

blocks.label: If you care most about a timely, efficient ruling

units.t: The PSC's staff says an early dismissal "will not serve the Commission’s objective of timely and efficiently resolving the issue."
The people who filed say the Cogeneration Act puts VoltaGrid under the PSC's power.
Georgia EMC says the PSC can enforce the Territorial Act apart from its power to regulate utilities.
Georgia Power says VoltaGrid's service "should be regulated by the Commission."
The PSC's staff asked that the dismissal decision wait until after the hearing.
On whether the people who filed may bring the case, Georgia EMC took no position and Georgia Power did not answer that point.
The number of filers does not decide the legal question, and the PSC has not ruled as of Nov 14, 2026.

subs.title: Outcome A: End the case with no ruling against VoltaGrid

units.t: The PSC would end the case with no ruling against VoltaGrid's plan, either by dismissing the case now or by finding after the hearing that the PSC has no power over VoltaGrid, that the people who filed may not bring the case, or that no law is broken.
units.note: the results VoltaGrid asks for (P-041, P-042) and the hearing questions (P-021)

units.t: VoltaGrid gives two grounds for dismissing now.
First, VoltaGrid says the PSC has no power over a company that does not serve the public.
Second, VoltaGrid says the people who filed are not "interested parties."
VoltaGrid and Serverfarm, the data center's owner, would face no PSC order in this case.
units.note: follows from the petition's requests (P-035) not being granted

units.t: The people who filed say neighbors would live with the plant's noise, light and air pollution.
Georgia EMC says a supplier's other consumers could absorb the cost of lines built for customers who are "picked off."
Georgia EMC's statement is about suppliers' lines in general; no filing we read ties it to this site or gives an amount.

The PSC would then order VoltaGrid to stop the work that breaks the law.
The people who filed, who say the plant adds pollution to their area.
Georgia Power says the site is in its assigned territory and Serverfarm is slated to become its customer.

units.t: Cards run in this order: the petitioners, VoltaGrid's two arguments, the two utility-side parties, then the PSC's staff; the order is not a ranking.
units.note: order of the cards

subs.title: 1. The petitioners say the plan is a power sale VoltaGrid has no right to make

units.t: The petitioners say VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, would sell power to Serverfarm, the data center's owner, in Georgia Power's area, breaking the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
Evidence: Mixed.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: The petitioners, a Newton County nonprofit and nearby residents, made the argument in the petition filed with the PSC on Jul 13, 2026.
units.note: the petition was filed Jul 13 (P-002); it names the nonprofit (P-029) and residents who live about two miles and less than 5 miles from the plant (P-030, P-031); their names and roads are left out under our privacy rule

units.t: The petition says: "The Territorial Act prohibits VoltaGrid from furnishing retail electric service to Serverfarm."
The petition also says the plan breaks the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners, because VoltaGrid "is selling its energy to Serverfarm."
The petition says: "Serverfarm and VoltaGrid are separate companies with no cross ownership or direct control over each other’s operations."

A witness for the PSC's staff said on Nov 13, 2026, that the contract's statement of work "states Monthly Fees per kWh" of a blacked-out amount, "with cumulative Monthly Fees increasing as the installation scales."
A VoltaGrid executive said in a sworn statement filed with VoltaGrid's Sep 16, 2026, request to dismiss: "VoltaGrid will not sell that electricity to Serverfarm or to anyone else."
The executive also said Serverfarm pays based on "the Conversion Assets’ producing capacity in operation, rather than a fee per kWh of energy."
VoltaGrid said on Oct 26, 2026, that every ban in the Territorial Act applies only to electric suppliers, and VoltaGrid says it is not one.
The fee amounts in the contract are blacked out in the public copy we read.

The PSC staff's witness said, about the contract terms the witness cited: "I am not a lawyer and do not have an opinion as to whether, standing alone, they resolve any legal classification under Georgia law."

Whether VoltaGrid's deal with Serverfarm, which VoltaGrid describes as a service and the petitioners describe as a power sale, is a retail sale of electricity is a legal question the PSC has not decided as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: process note; the Nov 4 order says the electric-supplier question is undecided (P-025)

cardMeta.evidence: Legal question (whether the deal is a retail sale); Mixed (the petition says VoltaGrid is selling its energy; VoltaGrid's executive says VoltaGrid will not sell electricity); Uncertain (fee terms are blacked out)

subs.title: 2. VoltaGrid says the PSC has no authority over a company that serves one customer on that customer's site

units.t: VoltaGrid describes its plant as an "on-site generator privately serving the owner of the site," not a service to the public, and says the PSC has no authority over VoltaGrid.
Evidence: Mixed.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: VoltaGrid made the argument in the brief it filed with the PSC on Sep 16, 2026.
The brief says VoltaGrid does not "furnish service to the public."
A VoltaGrid executive gave the same answer in testimony dated Oct 9, 2026.
The executive's sworn statement says Serverfarm supplies the gas and "VoltaGrid will not take ownership of the electricity."
The statement says VoltaGrid is not "pursuing any additional customer or business in Georgia."
VoltaGrid's brief says VoltaGrid "has no special privileges, no condemnation power, is the antithesis of a monopoly."

Georgia EMC, a trade group for electric membership corporations (EMCs), said on Oct 16, 2026, that "VoltaGrid conflates" the PSC's power to regulate utilities with its power to enforce the Territorial Act.
Georgia Power said the same day that VoltaGrid's service "is a public service that should be regulated by the Commission."
The petitioners said that, under one reading of the Territorial Act, VoltaGrid breaks the law "regardless of whether VoltaGrid qualifies as an electric supplier."
The petitioners said on Oct 16, 2026, that VoltaGrid "has explored serving other Georgia customers."

The PSC staff's witness said the contract's statement of work calls for "phased Power Delivery reaching 90 MW" and "states Monthly Fees per kWh" of a blacked-out amount, "with cumulative Monthly Fees increasing as the installation scales."
MW stands for megawatts, a measure of power, and kWh for kilowatt-hours, a measure of energy.
units.note: plain-language definitions, not from the cited sources

units.t: VoltaGrid's executive had said the pay is based on capacity, "rather than a fee per kWh of energy."
A ruling: the Hearing Officer, the person the PSC appointed to hear the case, wrote on Nov 4 that the question "is central to this docket and nothing in this Order decides it."
Whether serving one customer counts as serving the public is a legal question the PSC has not decided as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: process note; the Nov 4 order says the question is undecided (P-025)

cardMeta.evidence: Legal question (whether one customer is "the public"); Mixed (VoltaGrid says it seeks no other Georgia customers; the petitioners say it explored serving others)

subs.title: 3. VoltaGrid says the people who filed are not the "interested parties" the law lets bring the case

units.t: VoltaGrid says the Territorial Act protects only Georgia Power, the supplier assigned to the site, so the nonprofit and the residents cannot bring the case.
Evidence: Legal question.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: VoltaGrid made the argument in the brief it filed with the PSC on Sep 16, 2026.
The brief says the petitioners "can assert no interest the Territorial Act was enacted to protect."
VoltaGrid said on Oct 26, 2026, that the petitioners raised the same concerns with the state Environmental Protection Division, "which issued the air quality permit."
The petition quotes the Territorial Act as letting the PSC act on the complaint of "any other interested party."
The petitioners said on Oct 16, 2026, that VoltaGrid's reading would let utilities "wield the Territorial Act as a weapon for private gain."
The nonprofit's witness said on Oct 9, 2026, that if Georgia Power were building the plant, "we would be coming to the PSC to express our concerns."
The PSC's staff said on Oct 16, 2026, that dismissing the petitioners before the hearing "will not serve the Commission’s objective."
Georgia EMC took no position on the point, and Georgia Power limited its answer to the PSC's authority.
A ruling: the Hearing Officer wrote on Nov 4 that dismissing the case on such grounds before a record is made "would be premature."
Who counts as an "interested party" is a legal question the PSC has not decided as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: process note; the filing list (S01b) shows no order on the motion to dismiss

cardMeta.evidence: Legal question (who counts as an "interested party")

subs.title: 4. Georgia EMC says the PSC can enforce the Territorial Act apart from its power to regulate utilities, and that other customers could absorb stranded costs

units.t: Georgia EMC, a trade group for electric membership corporations (EMCs), says the PSC can enforce the Territorial Act here, and that a supplier's other consumers could absorb the cost of lines built for customers who are "picked off."
Evidence: Uncertain.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: Georgia EMC made the argument in its response filed with the PSC on Oct 16, 2026.
The response says an investment "could become stranded (with the costs thereof to be absorbed by the electric supplier’s other consumers) if future customers in the area can be picked off."
Georgia EMC says its member EMCs serve about 5 million Georgians and may be affected by the decision.
No other filing we read backs the stranded-cost point with figures, as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: scoped to the filings and excerpts we read

units.t: VoltaGrid said on Oct 26, 2026, that the Territorial Act covers only companies "otherwise subject to regulation by the commission."
VoltaGrid said: "Georgia Power remains the exclusive public utility authorized to serve Serverfarm."
No filing we read gives a dollar figure for any cost to other customers, as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: scoped to the filings and excerpts we read

units.t: Whether suppliers would lose customers this way is a prediction, as of Nov 14, 2026.

cardMeta.side: Georgia EMC; opposes Outcome A on authority
cardMeta.evidence: Legal question (how far the Territorial Act reaches); Uncertain (no dollar figure in the filings we read)

subs.title: 5. Georgia Power says a one-customer exception could let unregulated power plants spread

units.t: Georgia Power says that if serving one customer puts a company beyond the PSC, such plants could spread across Georgia without oversight.
Evidence: Uncertain.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: Georgia Power made the argument in its response filed with the PSC on Oct 16, 2026.
The response says single-customer plants "could proliferate across the state."
Georgia Power says the Territorial Act aims at "efficient, economical, and orderly rendering of retail electric service."
The petitioners said on Oct 16, 2026, that VoltaGrid "has explored serving other Georgia customers."
VoltaGrid said on Oct 26, 2026, that an on-site generator serving the site's owner "does nothing to cause competition among public utilities."
A VoltaGrid executive's sworn statement says VoltaGrid is not "pursuing any additional customer or business in Georgia."
No filing we read counts other single-customer plants planned in Georgia, as of Nov 14, 2026.

units.t: Whether such plants would spread is a prediction, as of Nov 14, 2026.
units.note: claim type

cardMeta.side: Georgia Power; opposes Outcome A on authority
cardMeta.evidence: Legal question (whether one customer is "the public"); Uncertain (no count of such plants in the filings we read)

subs.title: 6. The PSC's staff asks to decide after the hearing; its witness says the contract describes an ongoing power service

units.t: The PSC's staff says the dismissal request can wait for the Dec 9 hearing, and the staff's witness says the contract has VoltaGrid generate and deliver power to Serverfarm.
Evidence: Legal question; Supported; Uncertain.
units.note: restates the label

units.t: The PSC's staff made the request in a response filed with the PSC on Oct 16, 2026.
The staff's witness testified "on behalf of the GPSC Public Interest Advocacy Staff."
The staff's witness filed rebuttal testimony on Nov 13, 2026.
The staff's response says dismissing early "will not serve the Commission’s objective" of settling whether the Covington project falls under the PSC's power.
The witness said the statement of work requires VoltaGrid to "operate and maintain the equipment" and to "staff the site around the clock."

VoltaGrid said in its emergency appeal, first filed Nov 9, 2026, that the Hearing Officer's order wrongly came before "resolving the issues of whether Petitioners have standing" and whether the PSC has power over VoltaGrid.
VoltaGrid's executive said VoltaGrid "will not sell that electricity to Serverfarm or to anyone else" and that the pay is based on capacity, "rather than a fee per kWh of energy."
The staff's witness said the statement of work "states Monthly Fees per kWh" of a blacked-out amount, "with cumulative Monthly Fees increasing as the installation scales."
The filing list shows direct testimony from the same witness, filed Nov 12, 2026.
We could not download that testimony.

P-015.text: November 24, 2026 The Parties are to confer in advance of the Pre-Hearing Conference, and exchange documents proposed to be used at hearing as exhibits.

P-018.text: December 9, 2026 The Hearing Officer, beginning at 10:00AM, will conduct a hearing in this proceeding.

P-019.text: Public notice of this hearing shall be given by the Commission on the Commission Calendar posted on the Commission website.

P-020.text: Pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 46-2-58, the Commission has appointed the undersigned Hearing Officer to conduct a hearing in this proceeding and to make findings of fact and conclusions of law and present the same to the Commission in the form of a recommended decision for adoption by the Commission.

P-021.text: The following matters are at issue in this proceeding and will be decided on the basis of facts and arguments presented at the hearing: 1)Whether the Commission has jurisdiction over VoltaGrid as an “electric supplier” under O.C.G.A. § 46-3-3(3), 2)Whether Petitioners are “interested parties” entitled to initiate their Petition, and 3) Whether VoltaGrid’s planned construction and operation of the proposed generating facility, and delivery of the resulting energy to the data center Serverfarm, violates O.C.G.A. §§ 46-3-1 through 15 (the “Territorial Act”) and/or §§ 46-3-50 through 56 (the “Cogeneration Act”). 4)Whether any action from the Commission on the matters at issue is necessary.

P-022.text: In addition to assigning the matter to a Hearing Officer, the Assignment “authorizes the Staff to issue discovery pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 46-2-57(a)” and instructed the Hearing Officer to set a “hearing on the issues set forth in the Petition and on whether Respondent is providing service or offering to provide service that is subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission and, if so, what if any action the Commission should take.

P-023.text: For these reasons, VoltaGrid’s request for a stay is DENIED.

P-024.text: IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that counsel for Petitioners are granted access to materials marked trade secret subject to a protective agreement; ORDERED FURTHER that counsel for Petitioners and VoltaGrid shall execute a protective agreement that reasonably protects and insures the confidentiality of the protected information. A copy of the protective agreement shall be filed in this docket by 4:00PM on November 12, 2026;

P-025.text: The first is whether VoltaGrid is an “electric supplier” under O.C.G.A. § 46-3-3(3), or otherwise engages in conduct governed by the Territorial Act. That question is central to this docket and nothing in this Order decides it.

P-026.text: The Hearing Officer does not dispute that these issues are essential to this case,8 but has indicated that summarily dismissing the case on such grounds before establishing and certifying a record on the issues would be premature and contrary to the direction of the Commission.

P-027.text: VoltaGrid, LLC, is in the advanced stages of building a 90-megawatt power plant to sell power to a neighboring data center, Serverfarm.

P-028.text: On July 2, 2026, the Environmental Protection Division issued a “Notice of Violation” to VoltaGrid for constructing its powerplant before EPD issued an air permit.

P-029.text: Sustainable Newton is a grassroots, community-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization headquartered in Newton County, Georgia.

P-030.locator: petition p.4, para. 4 (part of a sentence; the name and road are left out)

P-031.locator: petition p.4, para. 5 (part of a sentence; the name and road are left out)
P-031.text: in Newton County, less than 5 miles from VoltaGrid.

P-032.text: All Petitioners are interested parties in preventing small and medium sized power plants, including VoltaGrid, from emitting fossil-fueled air pollution in Newton County, when more efficient power generation is available from utility-scale plants. All Petitioners share the interest in minimizing the disruption to Newton County’s natural environment caused by building short- term power plants like VoltaGrid, which contributes air, light, and noise pollution to an area already overburdened by these industrial impacts. Petitioners are also interested parties in the fair and equal enforcement of the Territorial Act.

P-033.text: VoltaGrid plans to furnish electric power to Serverfarm, a large retail customer. VoltaGrid is not the designated electric supplier for Serverfarm’s property; Georgia Power is the primary electric supplier for Serverfarm’s property. VoltaGrid does not satisfy any of the conditions to serve as an electric supplier pursuant to the large-load customer choice exception described in O.C.G.A. § 46-3-8(a). The Territorial Act prohibits VoltaGrid from furnishing retail electric service to Serverfarm.

P-034.text: VoltaGrid is a cogeneration facility within the meaning of the Cogeneration Act: VoltaGrid owns and operates its power-producing engines; VoltaGrid is not using all of its electric energy; rather, VoltaGrid is selling its energy to Serverfarm, which is not a retail supplier of electricity whose rates are fixed by the Commission. The plain language of the Cogeneration Act subjects VoltaGrid to the jurisdiction or regulation of the commission and prohibits VoltaGrid’s sale of electric energy to another person.

P-035.text: (a) Determine and declare whether VoltaGrid, LLC is planning to construct and operate a power plant to furnish retail electric service in violation of the Territorial Act or Cogeneration Act; (b) Order that VoltaGrid, LLC cease and desist any operations in violation of the Territorial Act or Cogeneration Act.

P-036.text: The Cogeneration and Distributed Generation Act of 2001 provides that “[a]ny person may operate a cogeneration facility without being subject to the jurisdiction or regulation of the commission if such person uses all of the electric energy, steam, or other form of useful energy produced at such cogeneration facility.” Id. § 46-3-53(a). It further commands that “[t]he electric energy shall not be sold to any other person” unless it is sold “to an electric supplier.
P-036.note: A page number (10) fell inside the sentence where the PDF page breaks; removed.

P-037.text: The Territorial Act provides that upon the complaint of “any other interested party, the commission shall have the authority and jurisdiction, after notice to all affected electric suppliers and other interested parties, and after a hearing, to enforce the provisions of this part by appropriate orders.

P-038.text: Serverfarm and VoltaGrid are separate companies with no cross ownership or direct control over each other’s operations;

P-039.text: Upon receiving this letter, the Company must stop all remaining construction of air pollution emissions sources and/or control equipment until such time that an air quality permit is issued for the construction and operation of the Facility.

P-040.text: VoltaGrid LLC proposes the construction and operation of VoltaGrid ATL-1 EGU, a greenfield power generation facility with a maximum power output of 90 MW, consisting of 33 natural gas-fired, four-stroke lean-burn (4SLB) reciprocating internal combustion engines (RICE), two (2) 4 MMBtu/hr natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters, and a natural gas-fired black start emergency generator. The facility will be a baseload facility, operating continuously for 8,760 hours per year.

P-041.text: As to the merits, VoltaGrid is not an “electric supplier,” as defined in O.C.G.A. § 46-3-3(3), and VoltaGrid is not (and will not be) engaged in the retail sale of electricity. VoltaGrid also does not “furnish service to the public” — a prerequisite to regulation under the Territorial Act — and thus is not subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction.

P-042.text: Because the only rights at stake under the Territorial Act belong to Georgia Power as the assigned electric supplier, Petitioners can assert no interest the Territorial Act was enacted to protect and they are not “interested parties” under O.C.G.A. § 46-3-13.

P-043.text: That balance does not apply in any sense to VoltaGrid, which has no special privileges, no condemnation power, is the antithesis of a monopoly, and is negotiating bespoke rates with a sophisticated counterparty.

P-044.text: I serve as Executive Vice President of VoltaGrid, a position I have held since October 2025.

P-046.text: Under the Serverfarm Agreement, Serverfarm supplies natural gas to the Serverfarm gas meter, and VoltaGrid will use the Conversion Assets to convert Serverfarm’s natural gas into Serverfarm’s electricity to be used by Serverfarm at its data center. Serverfarm will pay VoltaGrid for this service in amounts based on the Conversion Assets’ producing capacity in operation, rather than a fee per kWh of energy that the Conversion Assets actually deliver. 10. VoltaGrid does not purchase the natural gas that will be used by the Conversion Assets. VoltaGrid will not take ownership of the electricity that will be produced by the Conversion Assets, and VoltaGrid will not sell that electricity to Serverfarm or to anyone else.

P-047.text: The Georgia Constitution creates the Commission “for the regulation of utilities,

P-048.text: If Respondent’s interpretation is accepted, regulated monopolies, like Georgia Power, would get to wield the Territorial Act as a weapon for private gain, picking and choosing their competitors, which is in opposition to the Constitution’s limitations on monopolistic behavior.

P-049.text: Under this interpretation, VoltaGrid is in violation of the Territorial Act simply by furnishing retail electric service to Serverfarm without being either assigned or “chosen,” regardless of whether VoltaGrid qualifies as an electric supplier.

P-050.text: The Petitioners contend that the provision of such electrical service violates the Georgia Territorial Act, O.C.G.A. § 46-3-1 et seq., under which the right to provide electrical service is assigned to utility companies according to territorial boundaries established by the Commission.

P-051.text: Dismissing the Petition or the Petitioners from this docket before the scheduled hearing will not serve the Commission’s objective of timely and efficiently resolving the issue of whether Voltagrid’s Covington project falls under the Commission’s jurisdiction or is subject to the Territorial Act.

P-052.text: Wherefore, Staff requests that the Hearing Officer reserve making a decision as to Voltagrid’s Motion to Dismiss until after the December 9, 2026 hearing in this matter. This 16th day of October, 2026.

P-053.text: VoltaGrid conflates the Commission’s regulatory jurisdiction over public utilities with the Commission’s jurisdiction to enforce the provisions of the Territorial Act.

P-054.text: Georgia EMC takes no position herein on VoltaGrid’s standing argument.

P-055.text: The same is true if an electric supplier makes investments in lines and electrical facilities in anticipation of serving future load in its assigned territory. That investment could become stranded (with the costs thereof to be absorbed by the electric supplier’s other consumers) if future customers in the area can be picked off by a power supplier serving less than a significant segment of the public.

P-056.text: Georgia Power’s response is limited to the second contention, which provides no basis for dismissal.

P-057.text: Under VoltaGrid’s proposed rule, however, this orderly service would be threatened. Any entity, whether the recipient of an assigned territory under the Territorial Act or not, could “pop up” in Georgia, render any amount of service, and avoid Commission jurisdiction so long as they serve only one customer in the state.

P-058.text: VoltaGrid’s service of electricity to Serverfarm is a public service that should be regulated by the Commission. Failure to do so could lead to deregulation of the electric industry in Georgia as “pop-up” generation facilities serving single customers could proliferate across the state.

P-059.text: The Territorial Act divides the state of Georgia into assigned and unassigned territories, providing electric suppliers with specific monopolies over their assigned territory.33 The provision of these territories helps accomplish the Territorial Act’s policy goals of, among other things, assuring “efficient, economical, and orderly rendering of retail electric service”; inhibiting the duplication of electric supplier lines; and protecting and conserving lawfully constructed lines.

P-060.text: Georgia Power is a vertically integrated electric utility regulated by the Commission that serves approximately 2.6 million retail customers across more than 57,000 square miles of assigned electric service territory in Georgia.

P-061.text: Respondent seeks to provide bridge power to Serverfarm— an entity slated to become a Georgia Power customer—at premises situated squarely within Georgia Power’s assigned service territory as designated under the Territorial Act.

P-062.text: Georgia EMC is a statewide trade association serving the needs of Georgia’s forty-one electric distribution cooperatives that provide retail electric service in Georgia (“EMCs”). Georgia EMC is a not-for-profit, member-owned organization controlled by a board of directors elected by its members. The EMCs provide retail electric service to approximately 5 million Georgians.

P-063.text: The interests of Georgia EMC and its member EMCs may be substantially affected by any decisions reached by the Commission in this proceeding.

P-064.text: An on-site generator privately serving the owner of the site does nothing to cause competition among public utilities; it does not, for example, put one utility’s lines in another’s territory. Georgia Power remains the exclusive public utility authorized to serve Serverfarm.

P-065.text: This is demonstrably false, given that Petitioners raised the same concerns in another public regulatory agency: the Georgia Environmental Protection Division (“EPD”), which issued the air quality permit for VoltaGrid’s project.

P-066.text: Every prohibition in the Territorial Act runs to “electric suppliers.”[fn55] In addition, the Act’s statement of policy itself says it binds “electric suppliers” and mentions no one else.[fn56] Finally, the Act specially defines the term “electric supplier” as “any electric light and power company otherwise subject to regulation by the commission.

P-069.text: Q. Does VoltaGrid furnish service to the public in Georgia? A. No.

P-070.text: When looking at VoltaGrid’s arrangement with Serverfarm, if Georgia Power was building the power plant to provide electricity, we would be coming to the PSC to express our concerns – because Georgia Power is regulated by the PSC under Georgia law. But now we face the concerns discussed above as a result of the actions of a different energy company – one seeking to operate like an electric utility, while carving out a gray area they argue is outside the purview of the PSC.

P-081.text: The Order improperly requires VoltaGrid to execute a Protective Agreement and disclose its Protected Information to Petitioners before resolving the issues of whether Petitioners have standing to pursue a claim under the Territorial Act and whether this Commission even has jurisdiction over VoltaGrid.

Separate AI checkers, which never saw the drafting, then checked it: each sentence against the passages it cites, one whole-page read against all the passages, and fairness reviews from each side's seat. In this trial, no person checked the facts. Here is what the checkers did, what they found, and what is still open.

A panel of three reviewers read the first draft: one for VoltaGrid's positions, one for the people who filed and the parties opposing dismissal, and a neutral editor. After the fixes, a fourth reviewer read the page from each side's seat.
